summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment on qualified-immunity grounds, the court held prospectively that the Fourth Amendment governs child-abuse investigations, that the government may not seize a child absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, and that an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely justify seizing a child.
key_cases.relevance: The case Mississippi Section 1983 plaintiffs must satisfy: no court order, no consent and no exigency means an unconstitutional seizure.
key_cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworker who removed two boys not named in the court order and with no evidence of imminent danger, holding that requirement was clearly established before Gates, while reversing as to the search and the supervisor.
key_cases.relevance: Denial of qualified immunity here is the clearest Fifth Circuit example of a removal that crossed the constitutional line.
key_cases.quote: Gates was not required to give social workers fair notice that imminent danger must exist before a child may be removed without a warrant or court order

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a teacher who fabricated evidence of sexual abuse, causing a three-year removal and state-initiated termination proceedings, violated the clearly established right to family integrity and was not entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the substantive-due-process theory, distinct from the Fourth Amendment, for a prolonged wrongful separation.
key_cases.quote: We therefore hold that Plaintiffs' claims fall squarely within the well established constitutional right to family integrity and to be free of arbitrary, oppressive governmental action.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court remanded the procedural-due-process claim against the caseworker while rejecting the claims against the officers, holding it is clearly established that a court order or exigency is the predeprivation process due before a child is removed.
key_cases.relevance: Current Fifth Circuit framing of the wrongful-removal claim as procedural due process rather than only Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.quote: It is thus clearly established that a court order or exigency is the predeprivation process that is due when social workers remove a child.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed in part the denial of qualified immunity, holding that an unsuitable living situation, without evidence of imminent danger, is not exigency justifying a warrantless removal.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms in 2024 that the Gates standard remains clearly established law for wrongful-removal suits in Mississippi's circuit.
key_cases.quote: Unsuitable as R.B.’s living situation may have been, it did not constitute exigent circumstances necessitating warrantless removal from his mother.
